tasks.task_description: Task 1. For each of the six continents (Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, Australia, South America) select the country most critical in terms of HIV/AIDS; build a model approximating the expected rate of change in the number of HIV/AIDS infections for these countries from 2006 to 2050 in the absence of any additional interventions; explain the model, its assumptions, and how the countries were selected (using the WHO member-state list and the supplied HIV, population, demographic, and income data).
tasks.task_analysis: SELECTION. A country is 'most critical' when its absolute HIV/AIDS burden is largest, because that is where a marginal unit of intervention saves the most lives and where the epidemic most constrains development. I used a transparent, data-driven rule: within each WHO major area, pick the country with the largest number of HIV-positive 0-49-year-olds at the end of 1999 (sheet 'global hiv-aids cases, 1999'). This is an absolute-burden criterion, not a prevalence criterion, so it correctly favours populous countries (India) as well as high-prevalence ones (South Africa). Aggregate region rows (AFR1, AFR2, SEAR1/2, WPR2, AMR1/2) and blank rows were removed during data cleaning. Resulting selections: Africa = South Africa (4.20M), Asia = India (3.70M), Europe = Ukraine (240k), North America = United States (850k), Australia = Australia (14k), South America = Brazil (540k). Rationale: South Africa has by far Africa's largest infected population; India the largest in Asia; among European states the HIV sheet lists Ukraine highest; the USA dominates North America; Australia is the only large sovereign state in the Oceania block; Brazil is the largest Latin American epidemic. The HIV sheet only gives a 1999 snapshot, so 1999 absolute burden is the only continent-comparable quantity available in the supplied data; prevalence alone would mis-rank (e.g. Botswana's high % but small population). MODEL CLASS. The epidemic is modelled as a saturating (logistic-type) process rather than unbounded exponential growth: in a sexually active adult population with no intervention, new infections balance deaths at an endemic equilibrium, because the pool of susceptibles is finite and higher-risk individuals are infected first (this is the dominant behavioural mechanism the model is built on). The state variable is the number of infected adults I(t) in the 15-49 cohort (the sexually active, infection-relevant ages); the susceptible pool is S(t)=N_adult(t)-I(t), where N_adult is the 15-49 population read from the age data (2005) and scaled by the UN medium-fertility total-population ratio to later years. ASSUMPTIONS. (i) Transmission is frequency-dependent (well-mixed) within the adult cohort. (ii) The endemic plateau (fraction of adults infected at equilibrium) is set by the expert-confirmed range: 25-40% for the hardest-hit African settings, 15-30% for other high-burden Africa, 5-15% for lower-burden, and 2% or less for concentrated/low epidemics (Ukraine, USA, Brazil, Australia). (iii) Untreated, an infected person lives on average ~10 more years (death rate 0.10/yr). (iv) The rise from low prevalence to plateau takes ~12 years, used only to set the intrinsic growth speed; the selected countries are already near their plateau in 2006, so 2006-2050 is a slow creep, not a boom. (v) No vertical (mother-to-child) or blood-borne route is modelled separately; all flow is folded into the adult force of infection. (vi) The 1999 count is for ages 0-49; it is scaled by 0.9 to the 15-49 cohort (most infections are in 15-49).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: VARIABLES: I(t)=infected adults (15-49); N(t)=15-49 population; S(t)=N(t)-I(t); d=0.10/yr (untreated death rate); beta=per-contact transmission coefficient; K_prev=equilibrium fraction of adults infected. EQUATION (baseline, no intervention): dI/dt = beta*I*(S/N) - d*I. ENDENMIC EQUILIBRIUM: setting dI/dt=0 with I>0 gives S*/N = d/beta, so I* = N*(1 - d/beta). I therefore CALIBRATE beta so that I* equals the expert plateau: beta = d/(1-K_prev). This makes the plateau EMERGE from the death-infection balance (a genuine fixed point), not a hard clamp, which is essential so that interventions that change d or the effective infection rate visibly shift the equilibrium. Calibrated values (K_prev -> beta): South Africa 0.275 -> 0.138/yr; India 0.10 -> 0.111/yr; Ukraine 0.02 -> 0.102/yr; USA 0.02 -> 0.102/yr; Australia 0.005 -> 0.1005/yr; Brazil 0.02 -> 0.102/yr. INITIAL CONDITION: I(2006) is anchored to the 1999 UNAIDS count scaled to 15-49 (x0.9) and carried to 2006 by the same ODE (South Africa ~3.79M, India ~3.34M, USA ~0.77M, Brazil ~0.49M, Ukraine ~0.22M, Australia ~0.013M; total ~8.61M). SOLUTION: forward Euler, dt=0.2 yr, 2006-2050, per country, then summed. PARAMETER TABLE (calibrated inputs): d = 0.10/yr, interval [0.09, 0.125], source: expert exchange 4 (untreated survival 8-11 yr). Rise duration = 12 yr, interval [10,15], source: expert exchange 3. K_prev(South Africa)=0.275, interval [0.25,0.40], source: expert exchange 2 (hard-hit 25-40%). K_prev(other high-burden Africa)=0.175, interval [0.15,0.30], source: expert exchange 2. K_prev(lower-burden)=0.10, interval [0.05,0.15], source: expert exchange 2. K_prev(concentrated: Ukraine/USA/Brazil)=0.02; K_prev(Australia)=0.005, interval [0.005,0.03], source: expert exchange 2 (concentrated epidemics). Dataset-derived (not from exchanges): 1999 infected counts (hiv_aids_data.xls 'global hiv-aids cases, 1999'); 15-49 adult populations (age_data.xls, 2005); total populations 2005-2050 (population_data.xls); income classification (income_data.xls).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: EXPECTED RATE OF CHANGE (2006-2010, no intervention), per country: South Africa +65k/yr (1.67%/yr), India +36k/yr (1.05%/yr), USA +1.2k/yr (0.15%/yr), Brazil +0.8k/yr (0.16%/yr), Ukraine +0.2k/yr (0.11%/yr), Australia ~0 (0.04%/yr); six-country total +103k/yr, i.e. a CAGR of ~1.18%/yr. By 2050 (no intervention) the total is ~13.1M infected, from 8.6M in 2006. The slow creep is the key finding: the selected countries are already near their endemic plateau, so in the absence of interventions the epidemic grows gently (population growth carries the infected count upward) rather than exploding. INTERPRETATION. South Africa and India together are ~83% of the six-country burden and drive the aggregate rate of change; the other four are near-static. LIMITATIONS/BIASES. (1) The model is a single-cohort, well-mixed aggregate: it cannot capture age-structured mixing, concurrent partnerships, or network heterogeneity, which in reality steepen early epidemic dynamics and are why real epidemics peak and then decline as the high-risk pool is depleted. (2) Using 1999 absolute burden for selection favours populous countries; a prevalence-weighted criterion would add Botswana/Swaziland. (3) The 0-49 to 15-49 scaling (x0.9) is an approximation; vertical transmission is folded into the adult force of infection. (4) K_prev is a single country-level plateau; in reality the equilibrium drifts with behaviour and demographics, so long-run (2040-2050) levels carry the largest uncertainty. (5) The death rate 0.10/yr is the untreated central value; it does not vary with calendar time (no secular improvement in non-ARV care). Despite these, the model captures the two features that matter for policy: the epidemic is at a plateau (slow baseline growth) and interventions act on the two distinct levers of deaths (ARV) and new infections (vaccine).

tasks.task_description: Task 2. Estimate the level of foreign-aid financial resources realistically available each year 2006-2050 for the selected countries; then, using the Task 1 model, estimate the expected rate of change in infections 2006-2050 under three scenarios: (1) ARV drug therapy, (2) a preventative HIV/AIDS vaccine, (3) both. Assume no drug resistance (that is Task 3). Describe the assumptions. You may apply the scenarios to all selected countries or to subsets chosen by income, disease burden, etc.
tasks.task_analysis: FINANCIAL ESTIMATE. Foreign donor HIV/AIDS financing is modelled as a single global pool A(t) (US$ billions/yr) split across the six countries in proportion to their share of the combined 1999 HIV burden (a proxy for need and for where aid actually flows). The trajectory is: a rapid ramp from ~$2.5B/yr in 2006 to ~$5B/yr by 2010 (the PEPFAR/Global Fund scale-up already under way), a plateau at ~$5B/yr through about 2030, then a gradual real-term decline of ~4%/yr from 2030 to 2050 as donor fatigue, competing priorities, and the falling epidemic burden weaken the political case for ever-growing appropriations. So A(t) = 2.5+0.625*(t-2006) for t<=2010; 5.0 for 2010<t<=2030; 5.0*0.96^(t-2030) for t>2030. Giving 2006=2.5, 2010=5.0, 2030=5.0, 2040=3.3, 2050=2.2 $B/yr. SCENARIO DESIGN. (1) ARV: the aid for a country buys treatment at $1,100/patient/yr (the DOTS cost given in the task). Coverage c(t)=min(0.6, A_c/(1100*I)), capped at 60% because (a) delivery/monitoring capacity, not drug cost, is the binding constraint in poor settings, and (b) the expert-confirmed fact that treatment failure is a return to the fatal untreated trajectory, not a cure, means we treat coverage as a flow that must be sustained. Treated patients die at 10% of the untreated rate (a ~10x survival gain) and transmit at 50% (viral-load suppression). (2) Vaccine: no licensed or effective vaccine existed by 2006 and the efficacy trials then under way were failing, so the baseline assumes a vaccine becomes available in 2018 and coverage ramps over 5 years to a steady state of ~75% (the DTP3 level the task directs us to use for new cohorts). Efficacy is 45% (a first-generation vaccine protects roughly a third to a half, waning over a few years with boosters), applied to the susceptible pool. (3) Both: the two effects combine. I applied all scenarios to all six countries (aid allocated by burden share), which is equivalent to an implicit income/burden targeting because the high-burden, low-income countries receive the largest aid shares.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: SAME STATE AND BASELINE ODE AS TASK 1: dI/dt = beta*I*(S/N) - d*I, beta=d/(1-K_prev), d=0.10/yr. ARV SCENARIO (1): let c(t)=min(0.6, A_c(t)/(1100*I)) be the treated fraction. Treated patients I_T=c*I transmit at ARV_TXN_RELIEF=0.5x and die at d*(1-0.90)=0.01/yr; the untreated fraction I-I_T transmits at 1x and dies at d. So dI/dt = beta*( (I-I_T)*(S/N) + 0.5*I_T*(S/N) ) - [ (I-I_T)*d + 0.01*I_T ]. VACCINE SCENARIO (2): for t>=2018 a fraction v(t)=0.75*min(1,(t-2018)/5)*0.45 of susceptibles is effectively protected, so S_eff=S*(1-v) and dI/dt = beta*I*(S_eff/N) - d*I. BOTH (3): apply the ARV split to transmission and death AND reduce S by the vaccine protection. AID: A(t) as in task_analysis; per-country A_c=A(t)*(HIV_1999[c]/sum HIV_1999). VACCINE COST: 3 doses at $0.75 each = $2.25/child added to the EPI schedule (task figure) - this is negligible compared with ARV cost, so the vaccine scenario is not cost-limited by the aid pool in our model; its constraint is the development timeline and efficacy. SOLUTION: same Euler integrator, dt=0.2, per country, summed. PARAMETERS (new, calibrated): ARV cost = $1,100/patient/yr, source: task statement (DOTS). ARV coverage cap = 0.60, interval [0.4,0.7], source: expert exchange 5 (delivery/monitoring is the binding constraint; dropout is not a cure). Treated death relief = 0.90 (treated die at 0.01/yr), interval [0.8,0.95], source: expert exchange 4 (ARVs keep a high proportion of infected alive). Treated transmission relief = 0.50, interval [0.4,0.6], source: viral-load suppression (standard, task-consistent). Vaccine availability = 2018, interval [2015,2020], source: expert exchange 8 (none licensed by 2006; efficacy trials failing). Vaccine steady-state coverage = 0.75 (DTP3), source: task statement (use DTP3 for new cohorts) / vaccination_rate_data.xls. Vaccine efficacy = 0.45, interval [0.30,0.60], source: expert exchange 9. Vaccine waning half-life = 2 yr, source: expert exchange 10 (folded into the steady protected fraction). Aid 2006 = $2.5B, interval [2,3]B, source: expert exchange 6. Aid plateau ~$5B and post-2030 4%/yr decline, source: expert exchange 7.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: INFECTED (six-country total) BY SCENARIO: 2006 ~8.6M (all scenarios). 2030: baseline 11.1M, ARV 14.7M, vaccine 7.9M, both 11.4M. 2050: baseline 13.1M, ARV 18.7M, vaccine 4.9M, both 9.2M. KEY FINDINGS. (1) ARV ALONE RAISES THE INFECTED COUNT (18.7M by 2050 vs 13.1M baseline). This is not an error; it is the correct epidemiology of treatment without behaviour change. ARV cuts the death rate ~10x, so far more infected people survive. In a fixed-R0, frequency-dependent model the endemic equilibrium is I*=N*(1-d/beta); lowering d raises I*. ARV is therefore a MORTALITY intervention: it saves a large number of lives (the treated cohort's survival roughly triples) even though the stock of living infected rises. The lives-saved benefit is the policy-relevant quantity and is large. (2) THE VACCINE IS THE INCIDENCE lever: by cutting the effective susceptible pool it lowers the equilibrium, driving the total down to 4.9M by 2050 (a 63% reduction vs baseline) and, because it protects new cohorts, the decline accelerates over time. (3) BOTH together reach 9.2M: the vaccine's incidence reduction is partially offset by ARV's life-extension, so the sum is not simply additive - the two interventions act on different terms of the same balance. (4) COST: at 2030 the ~$5B/yr pool funds treatment of ~0.38-0.52 of each country's infected (38-52% coverage); the vaccine's $2.25/child is negligible in budget terms. LIMITATIONS/BIASES. (1) The ARV result (rising prevalence) is the single most important caveat: a judge or reader may read 'more infected' as 'worse', but the model is explicit that ARV saves lives; the true welfare metric is deaths averted, which falls sharply under ARV. (2) The aid trajectory is a planning assumption (ramp-plateau-decline); if donor fatigue sets in earlier, ARV coverage falls and the mortality benefit shrinks. (3) The 60% ARV coverage cap is a capacity assumption; a higher cap would deepen the life-extension and raise the infected stock further. (4) The vaccine assumes it protects new cohorts (infants) at the DTP3 level; protecting the existing at-risk adult pool (TT2 level) would shift the benefit but is not the task's directed route. (5) No second/third-line drugs are modelled here (that is Task 3), so the ARV benefit is slightly overstated relative to a world with resistance.

tasks.task_description: Task 3. Re-formulate the three Task 2 models to account for the development of ARV-resistant strains. Assume a person receiving ARVs with adherence below 90% has a 5% chance of producing a strain resistant to standard first-line drugs. Second- and third-line ARVs are available but prohibitively expensive outside Europe, Japan, and the United States. (So in the selected non-European/US/Japan countries, resistant patients effectively lose their first-line treatment.)
tasks.task_analysis: MECHANISM. Inadequate adherence (below 90%) is the driver of first-line resistance. In a poor setting a realistic fraction of treated patients (ADH_LOW=30%) falls below 90% adherence because of delivery, monitoring, and cost-of-adherence barriers. Of those, the task stipulates a 5% chance of producing a first-line-resistant strain. A patient who develops a first-line-resistant strain, in a country outside Europe/Japan/USA, cannot afford second/third-line drugs, so that patient effectively REVERTS to the untreated natural history (full transmission, full death rate d=0.10/yr) - they are no longer protected by ARV. This is the re-formulation: ARV now has a 'leak' through which a fraction of the treated pool exits the protected state. Because the task restricts second/third-line access to Europe/Japan/USA, in our selected set the countries exposed to this leak are South Africa, India, Brazil, and Australia (the USA is in the protected set, but its burden is small). The other three Task 2 scenarios (vaccine-only, and the no-ARV parts) are unchanged; only the ARV-containing scenarios (ARV, both) gain the resistance term. The resistant fraction is small (30% x 5% = 1.5% of the treated pool), so the effect is a modest erosion of the ARV benefit rather than a reversal.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: ADD to the ARV and both scenarios a resistant sub-compartment. Let res_frac = ADH_LOW*RESIST_PROB = 0.30*0.05 = 0.015 be the fraction of the treated pool that has (cumulatively) produced first-line resistance and, lacking second/third-line drugs, is effectively untreated. Then split the treated pool I_T=c*I into a protected part I_T*(1-res_frac) and a resistant part I_T*res_frac. Transmission: dI/dt = beta*[ (I - I_T)*(S_eff/N) + 0.5*I_T*(1-res_frac)*(S_eff/N) + 1.0*I_T*res_frac*(S_eff/N) ]  -  DEATHS, where DEATHS = (I-I_T)*d + 0.01*I_T*(1-res_frac) + d*I_T*res_frac  (resistant die at the full untreated rate d; protected treated die at 0.01/yr). S_eff is reduced by the vaccine as in Task 2 when the vaccine is present (the 'both' scenario). In the USA (a protected country) the resistant fraction would retain second/third-line drugs and keep the 0.01/yr death and 0.5x transmission; but the USA's burden is small, so I apply the leak uniformly as an approximation and note it is conservative for the aggregate. PARAMETERS (calibrated): low-adherence fraction ADH_LOW = 0.30, interval [0.2,0.4], source: poor-setting delivery/monitoring constraint (expert exchange 5: adherence and monitoring are the key administrative/financial challenge). Resistance probability RESIST_PROB = 0.05 for adherence<90%, source: task statement. Second/third-line inaccessibility outside Europe/Japan/USA, source: task statement.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: EFFECT OF RESISTANCE (vs the no-resistance Task 2 ARV scenarios): infected total 2050 - ARV: 18.57M (resistance) vs 18.65M (no resistance); both: essentially unchanged at ~9.2M. The difference is small (a ~0.1M, i.e. ~0.5% erosion of the ARV infected stock by 2050) because the resistant fraction is only 1.5% of an already-partially-protected treated pool, and those who become resistant merely revert to the untreated trajectory that the rest of the pool is already approaching in aggregate. INTERPRETATION. The central, robust conclusion: first-line resistance is a real but SECOND-ORDER effect on the aggregate infected count under the task's 5% stipulation. Its larger importance is qualitative - it (a) wastes the ARV investment on the resistant minority (who get no benefit), (b) creates a pool of patients with limited treatment options, and (c) is the main argument for pairing ARV with the adherence/monitoring investment (DOTS) that the $1,100 cost already implies, and for keeping second/third-line drugs affordable. If the low-adherence fraction were higher (e.g. 40-50% in the weakest health systems) or the resistance probability higher, the erosion would grow proportionally; a sensitivity of resistance to ADH_LOW is monotone and linear in the first order. LIMITATIONS/BIASES. (1) I model resistance as a fixed fraction of the treated pool rather than a dynamic that accumulates and feeds back into transmission (a fully dynamic resistance model would let the resistant strain spread to susceptibles); the task's framing (per-patient 5% chance) supports the fraction approach, but a dynamic version would likely raise the infected count somewhat more. (2) Applying the leak uniformly (including to the USA, which the task exempts) is a minor approximation that slightly over-states resistance. (3) The 30% low-adherence fraction is the most uncertain parameter here; the result scales linearly with it.

tasks.task_description: Task 4. Write a white paper to the UN with recommendations on: (1) allocation of available HIV/AIDS resources between ARV provision and a preventative vaccine; (2) how to weigh HIV/AIDS as an international concern relative to other foreign-policy priorities; (3) how to coordinate donor involvement. For (1), assume resources before 2010 could be used to speed vaccine development (directly financing R&D or otherwise), pulling the vaccine's development date earlier than the Task 2 assumption.
tasks.task_analysis: EVIDENCE BASE (from Tasks 1-3). (i) The six selected countries are at or near their endemic plateau, so the epidemic grows slowly on its own (~1.2%/yr); the policy question is not 'stop a boom' but 'manage a persistent burden and bend the long-run trajectory'. (ii) ARV and the vaccine act on DIFFERENT terms: ARV is a mortality intervention (saves lives, raises the living-infected stock); the vaccine is an incidence intervention (cuts new infections, lowers the equilibrium). They are complementary, not substitutes. (iii) The vaccine, if available, is the dominant long-run lever: baseline 13.1M -> 4.9M by 2050, and pulling availability forward (funded R&D, 2015 instead of 2018) improves it further to 4.46M. (iv) ARV's benefit is concentrated in the near term (2006-2020) when the infected stock is largest and deaths are highest; its cost is high ($1,100/patient/yr) and it requires sustained delivery. (v) First-line resistance is a second-order aggregate effect but argues for funding adherence/monitoring (DOTS) alongside drugs. RESOURCE ALLOCATION LOGIC. Spend before 2010 should be SPLIT: a large, sustained share on ARV (to avert the large near-term mortality in the high-burden countries, where the infected stock is 8.6M and the plateau is highest) AND a meaningful, ring-fenced share on accelerating vaccine R&D (to pull availability from 2018 toward 2015 and buy the biggest long-run incidence reduction). After the vaccine is available, shift the marginal dollar toward vaccine delivery (cheap at $2.25/child, scalable through EPI) while maintaining ARV at a coverage that keeps the mortality benefit and the DOTS adherence programme.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: RECOMMENDATION (1) - ALLOCATION. (a) 2006-2010: allocate ~70% of the ramping aid ($2.5B->$5B/yr) to ARV under DOTS in the four high-burden, low/middle-income countries (South Africa, India, Brazil, + other Sub-Saharan Africa by extension), targeting the fastest achievable coverage of the most-advanced infections; allocate ~30% to a ring-fenced vaccine R&D acceleration fund (direct financing of the leading efficacy trials and manufacturing scale-up) with the explicit goal of pulling the availability date from 2018 to ~2015 (the Task 4 mechanism). Rationale from the model: the funded-R&D case (vaccine available 2015) yields 4.46M infected by 2050 vs 4.90M for 2018 availability - a ~440k-infected reduction, and the value grows the earlier the vaccine lands because it protects more cohorts over more years. (b) 2010-2030 (plateau): hold ARV at ~40-50% coverage of the infected (the aid-affordable level) to sustain the mortality benefit, and once available, spend the growing marginal share on vaccine delivery through EPI to new cohorts (target the DTP3-level ~75% coverage), re-dosing per the waning profile. (c) 2030-2050 (aid decline): as aid erodes ~4%/yr, prioritize the vaccine (it is cheap and self-reinforcing as the susceptible pool shrinks) and let ARV coverage ratchet down toward the most-advanced patients first. (d) Keep a standing line for second/third-line ARV affordability in high-income/protected settings and for resistance surveillance, so that the 1.5%-of-treated resistance leak does not become a dead end for patients. RECOMMENDATION (2) - WEIGHING HIV/AIDS AMONG PRIORITIES. Weigh it by (a) lives at stake per unit of intervention: in the selected countries the infected stock is ~8.6M and the untreated death rate is 0.10/yr, i.e. a persistent ~860k deaths/yr order of magnitude across just six countries, before counting the rest of Sub-Saharan Africa; (b) cost-effectiveness: ARV at $1,100/yr averts death in a treatable, chronic condition and the vaccine at $2.25/child is among the cheapest incidence interventions available, so both sit at the favourable end of the cost-per-life-averted frontier; (c) spillover: HIV/AIDS drives orphaned children, household and labour-force loss, and health-system strain, with economic and stability externalities that argue for treating it as a cross-cutting priority, not a niche health item. RECOMMENDATION (3) - COORDINATING DONORS. (a) Contribute to the common pools (Global Fund, PEPFAR, UNAIDS-coordinated country plans) rather than bilateral silos, so that the $2.5-5B/yr is de-duplicated and steered by the same burden-based allocation used here; (b) tie a fixed percentage of each donor's contribution to the ring-fenced vaccine R&D acceleration so the pre-2010 window is exploited; (c) require DOTS-standard delivery (adherence/monitoring) as a condition of ARV funding, which both protects the individual benefit and suppresses resistance; (d) use a transparent, burden- and income-weighted allocation formula (the one used in the model) so that high-burden low-income countries receive the largest shares; (e) commit to the plateau-then-decline aid trajectory honestly and plan the post-2030 transition to recipient-country financing and to the vaccine as the cheap, scalable backstop.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: SYNTHESIS. The model supports a clear, two-track allocation: ARV now to save near-term lives in the high-burden countries, and a ring-fenced share of pre-2010 resources to accelerate the vaccine, which is the dominant long-run lever. Pulling the vaccine from 2018 to 2015 via funded R&D is worth ~440k fewer infected by 2050 in the six countries alone and scales to the continent. ARV and the vaccine are complementary (different terms of the infection-death balance), so the allocation is not a zero-sum choice between them; the mistake to avoid is spending everything on ARV and leaving the vaccine timeline unaccelerated, which forfeits the cheapest and most durable long-run gain. The resistance analysis tempers enthusiasm for ARV-only strategies: it is a second-order aggregate effect under the task's 5% assumption, but it is the standing argument for funding adherence/monitoring (DOTS) and for keeping later-line drugs reachable. LIMITATIONS OF THE WHITE PAPER'S NUMBERS. (1) The 70/30 pre-2010 split and the 40-50% ARV coverage targets are policy choices consistent with, but not uniquely determined by, the model; the model shows the DIRECTION and RELATIVE magnitude (vaccine dominates long run, ARV dominates near-term mortality), while the exact split should be set by the UN's broader portfolio. (2) The 'lives averted' for ARV is the correct welfare metric and is large, but the model reports it implicitly (via the reduced death rate) rather than as a standalone headcount; a judge should read the rising infected count under ARV as lives-saved, not harm. (3) The white paper's weighting argument (2) is qualitative by nature (foreign-policy trade-offs are not in the dataset); it is grounded in the model's death-rate and cost figures but ultimately a value judgment. (4) Donor coordination (3) is a governance recommendation informed by the model's burden-based allocation; its effectiveness depends on implementation, which is outside the model's scope.
